newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Eventful week ahead of payrolls.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Eventful week ahead of payrolls.

text.p: The bond market looked forward to a busy week culminating Friday with the critical May nonfarm payrolls report due on Friday.

In the interim the market will digest another report on manufacturing strength with the National Association of Purchasing Management's May report on Monday along with personal income and construction spending. Car and light truck sales also were to start to be released on Monday.
Leading economic indicators for April were scheduled for Tuesday and April factory orders on Wednesday.

"We'll just day-trade all week until the nonfarms come out. Some of the other numbers may be interesting, but we'll stay in recent ranges until we see payrolls," said a trader at a primary dealership.

Kevin Flanagan, vice president and money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc, said he thought the market might have gotten ahead of itself with sharp gains on Friday. He saw some corrective moves possible before payrolls.
"The slowing in April may have been an aberration. The true strength of the economy may start to surface in the May to June numbers," Flanagan said.
Flanagan said auto sales -- while not as strong as in March -- could rise back near the 7.0 million annualized level.
He suspected a number of temporary factors -- such as strikes -- tempered April's numbers and that NAPM and other data will show a snapback to continued strong growth.
Nonfarm payrolls likely would grow by 275,000, he said.

"It's going to be a week relatively decisive in shaping opinion on whether the Fed is likely to move at its July meeting," said Dana Johnson, managing director of research at First National Bank of Chicago.

Johnson said his firm was going to revise upward its estimate on payrolls growth until Bureau of Labor Statistics changed its seasonal calculations on Friday. He expected payrolls to grow by 220,000, unemployment to remain steady at 4.9 percent and a 0.5 increase in average hourly earnings.
"You would probably need something stronger than each of these numbers to create a higher probability the Fed will move," he said.
Lehman Government Securities Inc senior economist Cary Leahey said before BLS announced its new seasonal factors he would have said nonfarm payrolls would grow by 250,000.
However, with the revisions, he saw payrolls dropping to a 175,000 rise. "In the employment report we worry about a large rise in average hourly earnings -- anything above 0.4 percent, he said.
A contained payrolls report puts the likelihood of a further Fed tightening into August, Leahey said. "If we get that the market starts to feel good for itself," he said.
In addition, the dollar continued to be supported by the European Monetary Union seeming less likely to happen. There have been large flows out of European bonds into Treasuries in recent sessions.

German Finance Minister Theo Waigel's plan to revalue gold and currency assets set off a storm of criticism from the normally staid Bundesbank, and France was to hold elections on Sunday in which investors feared a victory by the left wing -- one that would undo many of the austerity measures put in place under President Jacques Chirac. These fears sent investors scurrying to the safety of U.S. Treasuries.
